content: Intravenous administration of 10 IU oxytocin is commonly used to prevent postpartum hemorrhage during vaginal delivery. The speed of administration varies significantly, ranging from a rapid bolus injection over one minute to a slower infusion lasting up to 40 minutes. The volume of dilution also differs, from 1 mL for bolus injections to 1000 mL of saline for infusions. However, there is no direct evidence comparing the effectiveness of these different administration regimens during vaginal birth. Clinical trials comparing slow intravenous administration of 10 IU oxytocin over one minute with intramuscular administration of the same dose have not raised safety concerns, such as hypotension or tachycardia. Observational studies in women undergoing cesarean sections, however, suggest that rapid intravenous administration can lead to adverse hemodynamic effects. Consequently, the Guideline Development Group recommends avoiding rapid injections and prefers that the 10 IU oxytocin dose be diluted and administered slowly. This recommendation is based on available evidence comparing intravenous and intramuscular oxytocin during vaginal delivery. For women undergoing cesarean sections, the World Health Organization (WHO) currently recommends a 10 IU dose of oxytocin for postpartum hemorrhage prevention, without specifying a preference for intravenous or intramuscular administration. This recommendation does not apply to other obstetric uses of oxytocin, such as labor induction, labor augmentation, or treatment of postpartum hemorrhage. The dissemination, adaptation, and implementation of this recommendation should involve all stakeholders in maternal healthcare at international, national, and local levels. It is essential to improve access to maternal healthcare and strengthen the capacity of healthcare facilities to provide high-quality services to all women during childbirth. This recommendation should be integrated into care packages and programs at the country and facility levels, where appropriate. Dissemination will occur through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, collaborating centers, United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. The recommendation will also be available on the WHO website and in the WHO Reproductive Health Library. Updated recommendations will be shared during scientific conferences and meetings attended by WHO maternal and perinatal health staff. The document will be translated into six United Nations languages and distributed through WHO regional offices. National and subnational groups may adapt and implement this recommendation based on existing strategies, which could include revising national guidelines or protocols. Global models, such as those for WHO antenatal and intrapartum care guidelines, can be tailored to different countries, contexts, and the specific needs and preferences of women. These models aim to improve maternal healthcare quality by achieving optimal physical, emotional, and psychological outcomes for women and their babies, regardless of existing policies within health systems. The successful implementation of evidence-based policies depends on well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes of adaptation and implementation. This may involve revising national or local guidelines and protocols, supported by ministries of health, United Nations agencies, professional societies, and other leadership groups. An enabling environment should be created to support the use of this recommendation, including changes in healthcare practitioners' behavior to adopt evidence-based practices. In humanitarian emergencies, adaptation of the recommendation should align with other response strategies and consider the unique needs, values, and preferences of women in such settings. Oxytocin should only be administered by skilled health personnel trained in the safe use of injectable uterotonics. While oxytocin is relatively inexpensive and widely available, it requires cold chain storage (2–8°C) to maintain its quality and effectiveness. In settings where cold storage cannot be guaranteed, the efficacy of oxytocin may be compromised. Despite some manufacturer labeling suggesting oxytocin stability at room temperature, this may not account for warmer conditions in certain countries, and different formulations have varying stability characteristics. To prevent degradation and maintain quality, oxytocin should always be refrigerated, regardless of labeling. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified knowledge gaps requiring primary research, particularly regarding the optimal intravenous oxytocin regimen for postpartum hemorrhage prevention after vaginal delivery. Implementing this evidence-based recommendation requires resources for sustainable procurement and storage of uterotonic drugs. Updating training curricula and providing training on the recommendation would enhance its impact and facilitate implementation. Standardizing care by incorporating this recommendation into intrapartum and immediate postpartum care packages can encourage behavior change among healthcare providers. Potential barriers to implementation include a lack of skilled personnel, resistance to adopting evidence-based practices, inadequate infrastructure (e.g., refrigeration), and insufficient supplies and equipment. Strategies to address these barriers are outlined in the implementation considerations section. Monitoring and evaluating the implementation and impact of this recommendation will occur at health service, country, and regional levels as part of broader efforts to improve maternal and newborn care quality. Data on the recommendation's implementation will be collected and evaluated to assess its impact on national policies. Interrupted time series, clinical audits, or criterion-based audits may be used to gather relevant data. WHO recommends using prophylactic uterotonic coverage as a process indicator for monitoring postpartum hemorrhage prevention. This indicator is calculated as the number of women receiving prophylactic uterotonics during the third stage of labor divided by all women giving birth. Additional locally agreed indicators may be necessary to assess care quality related to postpartum hemorrhage prevention and treatment. WHO has developed guidance for evaluating the quality of care for severe maternal complications, including postpartum hemorrhage, using near-miss and criterion-based clinical audit concepts. Monitoring the quality of uterotonic drugs in low-resource settings can guide healthcare personnel in selecting the most effective option for postpartum hemorrhage prevention. The recommendation will be reviewed annually by the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) to prioritize new and existing questions for development and updating. If new evidence emerges that could impact the current evidence base, the recommendation may be updated. If no new information is identified, the recommendation may be revalidated. Following publication and dissemination of the updated recommendation, any concerns about its validity should be promptly communicated to guideline implementers. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in the updated recommendation.
